introduction.heading: What is Git?
introduction.description: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes to files over time. Every clone of a repository is a full copy of its history, not just a pointer to a central server, which means you can commit, branch, and inspect history entirely offline, then sync with others - GitHub, GitLab, a teammate's machine - whenever you're ready.

concepts.title: Repository
concepts.description: A project folder plus its full history, stored in a hidden .git directory

concepts.title: Commit
concepts.description: A saved snapshot of the project at a point in time, with a message and a unique hash

concepts.title: Branch
concepts.description: A movable pointer to a commit, letting you work on something without touching main

concepts.title: HEAD
concepts.description: A pointer to whichever commit or branch you currently have checked out

concepts.title: Remote
concepts.description: A version of the repository hosted elsewhere - typically named origin - that you push to and pull from

concepts.title: Merge conflict
concepts.description: What happens when Git can't automatically combine changes to the same lines and asks you to decide

threeStates.heading: The Three States
threeStates.description: Every tracked file in Git sits in one of three places: the working directory (your actual files, as you edit them), the staging area / index (changes you've marked with git add, ready to be committed), and the repository (changes that are safely recorded with git commit). Understanding this pipeline - edit, stage, commit - explains almost everything else Git does.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Install Git from git-scm.com, then confirm it with git --version
Set your identity once with git config --global user.name and user.email
Start a new repo with git init, or copy an existing one with git clone <url>
Check what's changed at any time with git status and git log
Add a .gitignore before your first commit so build output and secrets never get tracked

practiceTopics.title: Clone & Remotes
practiceTopics.description: Copy a repository locally, then keep it in sync with git push and git pull

practiceTopics.title: Staging & Committing
practiceTopics.description: Move changes from the working directory to staging with add, then save them with commit

practiceTopics.title: Branching & Merging
practiceTopics.description: Work in isolation on a branch, then bring the changes back into main

practiceTopics.title: Rebase
practiceTopics.description: Replay one branch's commits onto another for a cleaner, linear history

practiceTopics.title: Stash
practiceTopics.description: Shelve uncommitted changes temporarily without making a commit

practiceTopics.title: Reset & Revert
practiceTopics.description: Undo history locally with reset, or undo it safely on shared branches with revert

practiceTopics.title: Cherry-pick
practiceTopics.description: Apply one specific commit from another branch without merging everything

practiceTopics.title: Resolving Conflicts
practiceTopics.description: Work through competing edits to the same lines when a merge can't auto-resolve

practiceTopics.title: .gitignore
practiceTopics.description: Tell Git which files and folders to never track in the first place

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: A typical feature workflow: branch, commit, sync, publish
fullExample.description: This is the day-to-day loop most Git users repeat constantly. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.
code: # 1. Get a local copy of a shared repository
# 2. Create a branch so main stays untouched while you work
# 3. Edit files, then stage the ones you want to commit
# 4. Record a snapshot of the staged changes
# 5. Bring in anything teammates pushed to main while you worked
# 6. Bring those updates into your feature branch too
# 7. Publish the branch so others - and a pull request - can see it

steps.label: Clone the repository
steps.explanation: git clone downloads the full repository, including its entire history, and checks out its default branch into a new local folder.

steps.label: Create a feature branch
steps.explanation: git checkout -b creates a new branch pointing at the current commit and switches to it in one step, so your changes stay isolated from main.

steps.label: Stage your changes
steps.explanation: git add moves a file's current changes into the staging area - a draft of exactly what the next commit will contain.

steps.label: Commit the snapshot
steps.explanation: git commit permanently records whatever is staged, along with a message explaining why the change was made.

steps.label: Pull the latest main
steps.explanation: git pull fetches new commits from the remote and merges them into your current branch - here, catching main up with what teammates pushed.

steps.label: Rebase your branch
steps.explanation: git rebase replays your feature branch's commits on top of the updated main, so the final history looks like you started from the latest code.

steps.label: Push the branch
steps.explanation: git push uploads your branch and its commits to the remote, making it visible to teammates and ready for a pull request.
